theme: With my whole heart I cry; your word is my hope
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 119:145-176. This is the last section of the longest psalm. It is a series of cries for help, and it ends in a surprising way. Read the last verse carefully.
settingTheScene: The final section of Psalm 119 is full of urgent prayer. The psalmist rises before dawn to cry out, and he prays at night. He is pursued by those who are far from God’s law, and yet he finds that God is near. The psalm ends not with a triumphant note, but with a confession that he has gone astray like a lost sheep, and a plea for the shepherd to seek him.
observation: “With my whole heart I cry; answer me, O LORD! I will keep your statutes” (v. 145).
“I rose before dawn and cried for help; I hoped in your words” (v. 147).
“You are near, O LORD, and all your commandments are true” (v. 151).
“The sum of your word is truth, and every one of your righteous rules endures forever” (v. 160).
“Great peace have those who love your law; nothing can make them stumble” (v. 165).
“I rejoice at your word like one who finds great spoil” (v. 162).
“Let my cry come before you, O LORD; give me understanding according to your word!” (v. 169).
“I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I do not forget your commandments” (v. 176).
interpretation:
The closing section is a prayer of desperate faith. “With my whole heart I cry.” The psalmist prays early in the morning and late at night. He is not casual about prayer. He is urgent, and he bases his urgency on God’s word: “I hoped in your words.” The word is the ground of his hope. He prays what God has promised, and he trusts that God will do it.

Verse 151 is a short statement of great comfort: “You are near, O LORD.” Surrounded by those who persecute him, the psalmist holds on to the fact that God is near. He does not say that his circumstances have changed. He says that God is close, and that is enough.

Verse 160 is a profound statement about Scripture: “The sum of your word is truth.” The whole of it, taken together, is truth. Each part is true, and the whole is more than the parts. It is a good verse to remember as you read the Bible as a whole. Each passage is a piece of a single truth.

The great promise of verse 165 is peace: “Great peace have those who love your law; nothing can make them stumble.” This is not the peace of having no problems. It is the peace of those whose lives are rooted in God’s word. Though they may be shaken, they are not toppled.

Then the final verse. After 175 verses about loving, keeping, and delighting in God’s law, the psalmist ends with, “I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant.” It is a moving confession. The most devoted lover of the word still needs a shepherd. He cannot keep the law perfectly. He needs God to find him. And he says, “I do not forget your commandments.” Even a lost sheep remembers the shepherd’s voice.

This is where the law leads: not to self-righteousness, but to a cry for a shepherd.
connection: Jesus told the parable of the lost sheep, in which the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to seek the one (Luke 15:3-7), and he said, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). Isaiah 53:6 says, “All we like sheep have gone astray… and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.” Peter says, “You were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25). The psalmist’s last prayer is answered in Christ.
application:
Pray verse 176 as your own. Admit where you have gone astray, and ask the shepherd to seek you.

Think about your morning and evening habits of prayer. Is there a small way to deepen them?

Spend time thanking God for the peace of those who love his law.
prayerPrompts: Cry out to God with your whole heart, telling him where you have gone astray.
Thank Jesus, the good shepherd who found you.
Ask him to keep his word near you.
